title: Class decorators

glossary.definition: Standard pieces of code that have to be written over and over again with little alteration, e.g., `def __init__(self, x): self.x = x`.
To change or alter the internal state or data of an object, e.g., `user.age += 1`.

overview.what:
A class decorator is a function that takes a class object as an argument and returns a modified class. Instead of modifying instances, it alters the class definition itself. The class name is rebound to whatever the decorator returns, applied once at definition time.

Think of it like a car factory adding a custom spoiler to every car model before any cars are actually produced.

When writing a class decorator, you can:

- Mutate the class directly to add attributes or methods
- Register the class in a global registry
- Return an entirely new wrapper class

Returning a wrapper class creates an identity trap that hides the original class metadata (like `__name__` and `__doc__`).

  def wrap(cls):
    class Wrapper: pass
    return Wrapper

  @wrap
  class Job: pass
  print(Job.__name__) # Prints 'Wrapper'
overview.why:
It reduces boilerplate when you need to apply the same structural changes across many classes.

Common use cases include:

- Adding standard methods like `__init__` or `__repr__`
- Registering classes to a central store or registry
- Enforcing class-level constraints

why_learning_this: Understand how `@dataclass` magically adds `__init__` and `__repr__` to your classes
Learn to register classes automatically upon definition

common_mistakes.title: Forgetting to return the class
common_mistakes.explanation: If your class decorator does not return the class object, the class name will be bound to `None` (or whatever you returned). This causes an unexpected `TypeError` when you try to instantiate it.

common_mistakes.title: Mutating the original class unexpectedly
common_mistakes.explanation: Class decorators usually mutate the class in-place and return it. If multiple parts of the codebase expect the unmodified class, this can cause hidden bugs.

recall_questions.q: What argument does a class decorator function receive?
recall_questions.answer: It receives the class object itself, not an instance of the class.

recall_questions.q: Why would you use a class decorator instead of standard inheritance?
recall_questions.answer: Class decorators are useful for applying standard modifications without enforcing a rigid inheritance hierarchy.

recall_questions.q: What happens if a class decorator returns a new wrapper class instead of mutating the original class?
recall_questions.answer: The class loses its original identity metadata, meaning `__name__` and `__doc__` will reflect the wrapper class instead of the original one.

challenge.title: Adding a class-level timestamp
challenge.prompt: Create a class decorator `add_timestamp` that adds a class attribute `created_at` to the decorated class. Set its value to `'2023-01-01'`. Apply this decorator to a class `Record` and print `Record.created_at`.

understanding_checks.question: What does this code print?
understanding_checks.why: The class decorator receives the class object, modifies its `value` attribute directly to `20`, and returns it.

understanding_checks.question: Why would you choose a class decorator over modifying instances directly in the `__init__` method?
understanding_checks.answer: Class decorators alter the class definition itself once (e.g., adding standard boilerplate or registering the class globally), rather than running logic every time a new instance is created.
understanding_checks.why: This reinforces the mental model that a class decorator modifies the blueprint, not the individual objects produced from it.
